headline: CISA flagged a self-spreading npm attack that tried to steal credentials.
discoveryQuestion: Who on your team installs npm packages? And how are your dev and CI tokens scoped and rotated?
avoid: Do not name affected packages or suggest the account was compromised. Package-level impact is not verified here.
sellerCaveat: Affected packages aren't verified; don't imply this account was hit.

roleNotes.note: A dependency that spreads itself makes package intake and install scripts part of the attack surface.
Dev and CI tokens on build machines are exactly what this kind of attack goes after.

headline: CISA reported attackers actively exploiting affected versions of SolarWinds Orion.
discoveryQuestion: How does your team decide which vendor updates to trust? Who owns that check?
avoid: Do not claim any product would have prevented it. The victim list and attack techniques are outside this record's verified scope.
sellerCaveat: Older incident (2020); victims and methods aren't covered here.

headline: Codecov said one leaked credential let an attacker change its Bash Uploader and pull data out of customers' CI environments.
discoveryQuestion: What third-party scripts run in your CI today, and which secrets can they see?
avoid: Don't say which customers lost secrets; that is not established.
sellerCaveat: Which customers actually lost secrets is unknown.

roleNotes.note: A vendor's script ran inside customers' pipelines, so anything those pipelines could read was in reach.
One leaked build credential reached into other companies' CI; build-time secrets need the same care as code.

headline: A popular GitHub Action had its version tags pointed at a malicious commit that printed CI secrets into workflow logs.
discoveryQuestion: Are your third-party Actions pinned to a commit SHA, or to tags that can move?
avoid: The 23,000 figure is repositories using the Action, not confirmed leaks.
sellerCaveat: About 23,000 repos used it; that's not a count of leaks.

roleNotes.note: Pinning Actions by tag wasn't enough; a tag can be repointed after you trust it.
Secrets printed into build logs are a leak path many teams don't watch.

headline: Malicious Nx packages turned developers' own AI coding tools into secret hunters. Wiz saw over a thousand valid GitHub tokens leak.
discoveryQuestion: Which AI coding tools run on your developers' machines? What can they read?
avoid: Don't present the initial token-theft route as confirmed.
sellerCaveat: How the publishing token was first stolen isn't confirmed.

roleNotes.note: Malicious packages now use the developer's own AI tools to search the machine for secrets.
Tokens and SSH keys sitting on developer laptops are the prize; how long they stay valid matters.

headline: Malware on one engineer's laptop stole a 2FA-backed SSO session. CircleCI told every customer to rotate their stored secrets.
discoveryQuestion: If your CI vendor asked you to rotate every stored secret today, how long would it take?
avoid: Don't claim specific customer impact; the source covers the rotation advice, not individual customers.
sellerCaveat: Impact on individual customers isn't covered.

roleNotes.note: One engineer's laptop led to every customer being told to rotate secrets; a vendor's incident becomes your rotation project.
Rotating every secret stored in a CI platform at once is the real cost; you need to know where they all are.

headline: Four credentials Cloudflare thought were unused, left unrotated after the Okta breach, let an attacker into Confluence and Jira.
discoveryQuestion: After a vendor breach, how do you find every credential that needs rotating, even the ones you think are unused?
avoid: Don't name an actor; attribution is Cloudflare's own assessment.
sellerCaveat: Attribution is Cloudflare's own; don't name an actor.

roleNotes.note: An incomplete credential list turned a vendor's breach into an intrusion at Cloudflare itself.
Service tokens and service accounts outlive the projects that made them; rotation needs a complete list.

headline: Per the FTC, intruders used reused passwords to get into a private GitHub repo, found an AWS key and reached Uber's S3 data.
discoveryQuestion: Do you scan private repos for cloud keys? Is MFA required on your code host?
avoid: This happened in 2016; don't present it as recent.
sellerCaveat: This was 2016; use it as a lesson, not news.

roleNotes.note: A key in a private repo is still exposed the moment someone gets into the repo.
An AWS key in code turned access to a code repository into access to cloud data.

headline: Microsoft reported an attacker used an acquired consumer signing key to forge tokens and get into Outlook Web Access and Outlook.com.
discoveryQuestion: Where do your signing keys live? How would you know if key material left that environment?
avoid: Don't state how the key was stolen; Microsoft has not confirmed it.
sellerCaveat: How the key left Microsoft is still unconfirmed.

roleNotes.note: One acquired key was enough to forge access to email accounts. Expect your board to ask who controls keys like that.
Keys that mint tokens need the tightest custody; where they live and who can reach them matters most.

headline: An admin GitHub token for Python's core organizations was sitting in a compiled .pyc file inside a public Docker image.
discoveryQuestion: Do your secret scans cover build artifacts and container images, or just source code?
avoid: PyPI found no malicious use; don't describe it as an attack.
sellerCaveat: No malicious use was found; this was an exposure.

roleNotes.note: Secrets can hide in build outputs like compiled files, not just in source code.
Public container images can carry credentials left over from the build that made them.

headline: One over-scoped Azure SAS token in a public GitHub repo exposed 38TB of private Microsoft research data.
discoveryQuestion: How do you keep track of the scope and expiry of shared-access tokens your teams create?
avoid: Wiz reported no attacker activity; describe it as an exposure, not an attack.
sellerCaveat: No attacker activity was reported; this was an exposure.

roleNotes.note: A share token scoped to a whole storage account turned sharing a few files into a much larger exposure.
Research and data-sharing repos need the same secrets review as production code.

headline: Exposed .env files handed attackers AWS keys. The campaign targeted 110,000 domains and pulled over 90,000 unique variables.
discoveryQuestion: Could one of your web apps expose its .env file? Would you notice if those keys got used?
avoid: Don't name an actor or a number of extorted organizations; neither is stated.
sellerCaveat: The actor and number of extorted orgs aren't stated.

roleNotes.note: Cloud keys in exposed web app config files were the starting point for an extortion campaign.
Deployment config files holding live keys are something attackers scan the internet for.

headline: Okta said an attacker used a support-system service account whose password had been saved to an employee's personal Google account. They read support files from 134 customers and hijacked sessions at 5 of them.
discoveryQuestion: When your teams send HAR files or logs to a vendor's support, are session tokens stripped first? Who checks?
avoid: Don't name a customer beyond those Okta itself named, and don't present the personal-account exposure path as confirmed.
sellerCaveat: How the password leaked isn't confirmed.

roleNotes.note: Files your team uploads to a vendor's support desk can carry live session tokens. Vendor support is part of your attack surface.
Troubleshooting files like HAR files can carry live session tokens; scrub them before they leave.

headline: Toyota said a contractor left a data server access key in public GitHub code for almost five years, putting up to 296,019 customer records at risk.
discoveryQuestion: Do your contractors' repos fall under your secret scanning, or only your own?
avoid: Toyota could not confirm the key was used; don't describe it as a confirmed theft.
sellerCaveat: Toyota couldn't confirm the key was ever used.

roleNotes.note: A contractor's public code held a live server key; third-party developers' repos are your exposure too.
A contractor's mistake left customer records at risk for almost five years. Their code is your liability too.

headline: An attacker used a contractor's bought password and kept sending MFA push requests until one got approved. From there they moved into Slack and G-Suite.
discoveryQuestion: Do your contractors use push-approval MFA? Would you notice a burst of denied prompts?
avoid: Don't repeat the hard-coded PAM credential story; Uber's statement doesn't support it.
sellerCaveat: Uber says it saw no access to production systems or user databases.

roleNotes.note: Two-factor gave way to a bought password and repeated push requests. Push-only MFA is worth raising with leadership.
Once inside, the attacker reached other employees' accounts with elevated permissions; internal access scope matters.

headline: Unit 42 reported that attackers ran an open-source AI pentest framework through 25 operations against at least 19 organizations, and got in at 10.
discoveryQuestion: If an automated agent scanned you today, what would it find first? Sprayable logins, exposed APIs, old CVEs?
avoid: Don't name victims or state attribution as fact; Unit 42's assessment is moderate confidence.
sellerCaveat: Victims are unnamed; the China link is a moderate-confidence assessment.

roleNotes.note: One tracked actor used AI tooling to work through many organizations at once, so expect attempts in volume.
Automated attack agents work through internet-facing weaknesses at volume; external exposure is the first place to look.

headline: West Pharmaceutical's SEC filing reported data theft and encrypted systems that disrupted its operations worldwide.
discoveryQuestion: If key systems were encrypted tomorrow, which operations would stop? How fast could you restore them?
avoid: Don't name a ransomware group or give impact figures; the filing names neither.
sellerCaveat: The filing names no attacker and no impact figures.

roleNotes.note: West had to report this in an SEC filing. For public companies, incident disclosure is now part of the CISO's job.
Encrypted systems disrupted operations worldwide; recovery time is the operational question.

headline: Binance said attackers reached its internal wallet-signing service; press summaries of its report say a deployment token on an engineer's laptop was a key step.
discoveryQuestion: Where do deployment and CI tokens live on your engineers' laptops, and would you notice one being used from the wrong machine?
avoid: Don't state a dollar figure or name an attacker; the report is preliminary and the amounts differ across reports.
sellerCaveat: Preliminary report; amounts and attribution aren't confirmed.

headline: Novo Nordisk said attackers got into a limited number of internal systems and copied non-public data, including personal data.
discoveryQuestion: If someone copied data out of a few internal systems, how quickly could you tell which accounts or credentials they used?
avoid: Don't repeat the extortion group's data volume or ransom figure; Novo Nordisk hasn't confirmed them.
sellerCaveat: How the attackers got in hasn't been disclosed.

headline: A sales tool's OAuth tokens let an attacker export Salesforce data from many companies, then mine it for cloud keys.
discoveryQuestion: Which third-party apps hold OAuth grants into your CRM, and how fast could you revoke them all?
avoid: Don't say Salesforce was breached; Google found the access came through Drift's tokens.
sellerCaveat: Google's report doesn't cover how the tokens were first stolen.

roleNotes.note: A trusted integration became the way in, with no phishing of your own staff.
Keys stored in CRM records were in the export, and the attacker searched it for them.

headline: One employee's GitHub token in a public repo reportedly opened Mercedes' internal code server for about four months.
discoveryQuestion: Would you know if a token for your internal Git server showed up in someone's personal repo?
avoid: Don't claim misuse; no attacker use was reported.
sellerCaveat: Exposure only; researcher and Mercedes disagree on access scope.

roleNotes.note: Personal repos are outside most org scanning but can hold work tokens.
Long-lived Git tokens with broad scope turn one leak into full code access.

headline: A worm in VS Code extensions stole npm, GitHub and Git credentials from developers and used them to spread.
discoveryQuestion: Do you know which editor extensions your developers run, and what tokens those machines hold?
avoid: Don't imply your customer was hit; Koi's counts are downloads, not confirmed victims.
sellerCaveat: Figures are from Koi's first report, October 2025.

roleNotes.note: Developer machines are now a supply chain entry point, not just the build.
Stolen publisher credentials let the worm push malicious versions of more extensions.

headline: A poisoned security scanner in LiteLLM's CI leaked its PyPI token, and two malicious releases stole cloud and Kubernetes secrets.
discoveryQuestion: What secrets can your CI security tools read, and who would notice if one of them was tampered with?
avoid: Don't blame Trivy's maintainers or name an actor; LiteLLM only says the compromise likely came through Trivy.
sellerCaveat: Malicious versions were live about 40 minutes on PyPI.

roleNotes.note: Publishing tokens in CI are reachable by every step, including security tools.
Anything that installed those versions should treat its cloud keys as stolen.

headline: Attackers decrypted environment variables for up to about 100,000 Railway workspaces and went after AI keys first.
discoveryQuestion: If your hosting provider asked you to rotate every environment variable tomorrow, how long would it take?
avoid: Don't quote the 1.85% as confirmed theft; it's Railway's upper bound.
sellerCaveat: Misuse estimate is Railway's own, about $740,000.

roleNotes.note: Secrets stored at a vendor share that vendor's breach.
Rotation speed decides the damage once a platform tells you to roll keys.

headline: Stolen internal credentials at Fireworks AI exposed API keys customers had stored in evaluation jobs.
discoveryQuestion: Which third-party AI platforms hold copies of your API keys, and who rotates them if one is breached?
avoid: Don't say customer models or prompts were accessed; Fireworks says it found no evidence of that.
sellerCaveat: Fireworks later disclosed a second, separate incident.

roleNotes.note: Keys copied into vendor job settings outlive the job.
AI vendors are now part of the secrets estate.

headline: Chainalysis says an attacker using agentic techniques exposed live tokens and password hashes for every user.
discoveryQuestion: If a vendor told you all your users' tokens were exposed, could you rotate every API key that day?
avoid: Don't describe the attack method beyond the company's 'offensive agentic techniques' wording.
sellerCaveat: Chainalysis first said no tokens were affected, then corrected it.

roleNotes.note: Early vendor statements can change; plan rotation before the final word.
API keys tied to a vendor need an owner and a rotation path.

headline: Northflank says an API flaw let an attacker decrypt customer secrets; the misuse reported so far is AI provider keys.
discoveryQuestion: If a platform you deploy on told you to treat every stored secret as exposed, how long would rotating them all take?
avoid: Don't say how the flaw worked beyond Northflank's description.
sellerCaveat: The disclosure date is approximate; don't give a specific date.

roleNotes.note: Northflank told every customer to treat every stored secret as exposed. You need a list of what you keep on platforms like it and how fast you can rotate it.
A deployment vendor's flaw exposed secrets for about 1.5% of its customer teams. Secrets you keep at a vendor are your exposure too.

headline: Apify says one compromised credential let an attacker collect more credentials and reach customer accounts.
discoveryQuestion: How quickly could you tell which of your internal credentials can unlock other credentials?
avoid: Don't describe the initial credential; Apify hasn't said what it was.
sellerCaveat: Apify's fuller report hadn't been found as of 2026-11-21; details may change.

roleNotes.note: One compromised credential led to more credentials and then into customer accounts. Ask vendors how they stop that kind of chain.
Apify had to revoke OAuth connections, including GitHub. Every integration you've authorized to a vendor needs an owner who can cut it off.

headline: Notion says credentials users pasted into AI chats were exposed through its AI vendor, so it revoked or reported them.
discoveryQuestion: Do you know which secrets your people paste into AI tools, and who those tools share data with?
avoid: Don't imply Notion's own systems were breached; the dataset was at its vendor.
sellerCaveat: Don't pitch secret scanning as the fix for pasting secrets into AI chats; the honest angle is finding and rotating secrets after they spread.

roleNotes.note: Secrets your people paste into AI tools can end up with the AI tool's own vendor.
Chat transcripts are a place secrets leak that code scanning doesn't reach.

headline: Zeabur says plaintext, non-expiring admin tokens in a config repo let an attacker read 3.2 million environment variable records.
discoveryQuestion: Where do your long-lived admin tokens live, and when were they last rotated?
avoid: Don't state how the attacker got the config repo; Zeabur only hypothesizes.
sellerCaveat: The 3,218,965 record figure is from Zeabur's preliminary report, marked confirmed there; the report may be updated.

roleNotes.note: Admin tokens that never expired, kept in a config repo, were the root cause. A token with no expiry turns one leak into lasting access.
Zeabur is shutting down after its second breach in two months. A vendor's incident can end the vendor, not just cost you a rotation.

headline: WorkOS says a weak development credential that also worked in production let an AI agent into its sales tool.
discoveryQuestion: Could a credential meant for local development authenticate against anything in your production?
avoid: Don't describe this as a leaked secret; it was a weak, predictable credential.
sellerCaveat: A weak, guessable credential isn't something a secret scanner reliably catches; don't claim a scanner would have stopped this.

roleNotes.note: A development credential that also worked in production let the attacker skip the line between them.
WorkOS says a researcher's AI agent escaped its test environment and got in. Agent experiments need the same access limits as people.

headline: Chainstack says default Grafana admin credentials led an attacker, step by step, to production secrets.
discoveryQuestion: If one dev tool kept its default password, what else could its machine credentials reach?
avoid: Don't call it a software vulnerability; Chainstack says none was exploited.
sellerCaveat: The disclosure date is approximate; don't give a specific date.

roleNotes.note: Default admin credentials on an internet-facing Grafana started the chain. Internal tools you expose need the same credential checks as production.
Machine credentials that worked in both dev and production let the attacker get from one to the other in three days.

headline: DreamHost says logins typed into its File Manager for about ten weeks should be treated as compromised.
discoveryQuestion: If a hosting provider told you ten weeks of logins were captured, which deploy credentials would you rotate first?
avoid: Don't name the vulnerable software; DreamHost hasn't.
sellerCaveat: The disclosure date is approximate; don't give a specific date.

roleNotes.note: About ten weeks of FTP and SFTP logins were captured. Deploy credentials typed into a host's web tools are only as safe as that host.
DreamHost found the access weeks after it began. Ask vendors how quickly they'd know.

headline: LiteLLM says a key deleted from a file but left in Git history, and never revoked, led to a poisoned release.
discoveryQuestion: When someone deletes a committed key, does your process also revoke it?
avoid: Don't imply any specific tool would have prevented it.

roleNotes.note: Deleting a committed key doesn't remove it from Git history. This one stayed usable for over four months because nobody revoked it.
One admin key led to maintainer tokens taken through CI, then a poisoned release on PyPI, Docker Hub and GHCR.

headline: GitGuardian says hijacked GitHub accounts pushed workflows built to steal repository secrets into hundreds, then thousands, of repos.
discoveryQuestion: Which secrets can your GitHub Actions workflows read, and would you notice a new workflow sending them out?
avoid: Don't give one total; counts differ by phase and source.
sellerCaveat: Only GitGuardian's summary was checked, not the full post; stick to the headline.

roleNotes.note: Hijacked accounts pushed workflows that read whatever secrets the repo's Actions could read. Workflow changes need review like code.
Secrets exposed to Actions are only as safe as every account that can push a workflow.

headline: Microsoft says AI agents are searching public GitHub for exposed secrets and using them to break into cloud tenants within minutes.
discoveryQuestion: If a secret tied to your company landed in a public repo today, would you find it before an automated search did?
avoid: Don't tie this to Storm-0940 or any named actor; Microsoft doesn't.
sellerCaveat: "Within minutes" is Microsoft's claim; attribute it to Microsoft rather than stating it as fact.

roleNotes.note: Automated searches comb public GitHub for credentials and AI keys tied to specific companies. Attackers may find your leak before you do.
Leaked app credentials were used to sign in as service principals and pull more secrets from Key Vault. Microsoft says one case took about five minutes.

headline: Lightning AI says unauthorized access to credentials took its platform offline in October.
discoveryQuestion: If an AI platform you use went offline over a credential incident, which of your keys stored there would you rotate?
avoid: Don't describe scope; Lightning hasn't published it here.
sellerCaveat: Only Lightning's post summary was read; scope and whose credentials were accessed are unknown.

roleNotes.note: An AI development platform went offline over a credential incident. Know which of your keys live on platforms like it.

headline: Nitori says up to 37.62 million customer records may have leaked after unauthorized access to its systems.
discoveryQuestion: When the entry point isn't known yet, how quickly can you tell what a breach could have touched?
avoid: Don't suggest a cause; Nitori hasn't named one.
sellerCaveat: No credential or secrets angle is reported; use only as general breach context.

roleNotes.note: Up to 37.62 million records may have leaked, and the cause isn't known yet. Early disclosures often lack the details you'd need to act.

headline: Ipsos says one internal system was breached; it hasn't said which or how.
discoveryQuestion: If a vendor disclosed a breach with no details, what would you ask them first?
avoid: Don't speculate on what was taken.
sellerCaveat: Very thin record with no secrets angle reported; a weak conversation opener.

roleNotes.note: Ipsos disclosed a breach of one internal system with no other details. Vendor contracts should say what you'll be told, and when.

headline: Cursor says a key it gave a vendor was exposed there, and unredacted credentials in old agent traces did the rest.
discoveryQuestion: Which keys have you issued to vendors, and do you know where those vendors store them?
avoid: Don't call it an Anthropic or Open VSX vulnerability; Cursor says it wasn't.
sellerCaveat: Fewer than 0.01% of Cursor customers had credentials exposed; don't overstate the scale.

roleNotes.note: A key Cursor issued to its AI vendor was exposed at the vendor. Keys you give vendors are still your keys.
Old coding-agent traces held unredacted credentials, and the attacker reused them. Agent logs need the same secrets hygiene as code.

headline: GitBook says one Cloudflare API key, found in internal code, turned a login flaw into full infrastructure access.
discoveryQuestion: Which API keys sit in your internal repos, and what would each one unlock?
avoid: Don't present the AI-agent detail as confirmed; GitBook calls it an inference.
sellerCaveat: GitBook couldn't tell whether the attacker acted inside customer repos; don't say customer code was touched.

roleNotes.note: A Cloudflare API key in internal repos turned a login flaw into full infrastructure access.
GitBook rotated every secret and invalidated customer API tokens. One key in a repo can mean a full rotation for you and your customers.

headline: Barracuda says a cloud key it gave a vendor years ago, and never retired, opened a 44-hour chain of stolen secrets.
discoveryQuestion: How many credentials have you given vendors for projects that are already over?
avoid: Don't name the vendor or attach Railway's $740,000 figure.
sellerCaveat: Barracuda's ARTEX match describes method, not actor; don't name an actor.

roleNotes.note: A key given to a vendor for a past project was never retired. In about 44 hours it led through roughly 10 cloud accounts.
The attacker made a build workflow print secrets into job logs. Logs are a leak path to watch.

headline: Wiz says a vendor's AWS credentials opened customers' old, unused integration roles, and the attacker read the secrets behind them.
discoveryQuestion: Which vendor integration roles in your AWS accounts are still trusted but no longer used?
avoid: Mention the attacker's use of open-source tools neutrally; don't imply any vendor involvement.
sellerCaveat: The attacker used open-source TruffleHog to check which stolen keys were live. If a buyer raises it, say plainly that attackers use open-source tools too; don't spin it. Wiz gives no victim count; "dozens" comes from Sentra.

roleNotes.note: Customers had roles in their AWS accounts that still trusted Qubole but sat unused, and the attacker used them. Old trust relationships need a review date.
One vendor's credentials opened many customers' accounts at once. Ask which vendors can still reach into yours.

headline: Aikido says 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts pushed a stealer that took CI secrets from at least 1,806 repos.
discoveryQuestion: If a contributor's account were hijacked, which secrets could a pull request reach in your CI?
avoid: Don't attribute this to the GhostAction actor; Aikido doesn't.
sellerCaveat: Repo counts differ by source (1,806, 1,835, 8,093); say "at least 1,806" and cite Aikido. The date is approximate.

roleNotes.note: Pull requests from hijacked accounts ran a payload that stole Actions secrets and cloud credentials. Limit what CI exposes to outside contributions.
Aikido says the count of at least 1,806 repos may be low because run logs were deleted. Keep CI logs long enough to investigate.

headline: Socket says a new Ruby gem stole cloud, CI and AI tool credentials the moment it was installed.
discoveryQuestion: Which credentials sit on the machines where developers install new packages?
avoid: Don't claim known victims; none are confirmed.

roleNotes.note: A clean first version, then a malicious one two hours later. Trust in a new package can't come from its first release.
The payload read 51 credential stores in one install. Developer machines hold far more keys than most teams think.

headline: Google says suspected North Korean actors edited Claude Code settings in victims' repos to plant a backdoor, and made GitHub tokens that looked like Copilot's.
discoveryQuestion: Would you notice a new personal access token in your GitHub org named to look like a trusted tool?
avoid: Don't call it a Claude Code vulnerability.
sellerCaveat: Attribution is suspected; keep that word. The attacker already had repo access and misused a settings file.

roleNotes.note: Editing an AI tool's settings file in a repo was enough to plant a backdoor. Config files for developer tools need review like code.
The attacker made GitHub tokens named after Copilot to blend in. Review new tokens by owner and scope, not by name.

headline: An attacker used TanStack's own GitHub Actions setup to publish 84 malicious versions of 42 npm packages in six minutes, with a payload that stole cloud, Kubernetes, Vault, npm and GitHub credentials.
discoveryQuestion: Could code from a fork reach the cache or tokens your release workflow uses?
avoid: Don't name an actor; TanStack doesn't attribute the attack.
sellerCaveat: TanStack says the attacker published with an OIDC token read from the GitHub Actions runner's memory, after poisoning a cache from a fork.

roleNotes.note: Fork-triggered workflows and shared caches let outside code reach release credentials. Keep release jobs separate from them.
Any machine that installed those versions in the window should treat the secrets it held as stolen.

headline: After the TanStack worm leaked credentials from Grafana's CI runners, Grafana rotated them but missed one, and the attacker used it three days later to copy its GitHub repositories and demand a ransom.
discoveryQuestion: After a leak, how would you prove every credential a compromised runner could reach was rotated?
avoid: Don't say customer data or Grafana Cloud was affected; Grafana says they weren't.
sellerCaveat: Grafana names the missed credential only as a bot identity (grafana-delivery-bot), not a token type. The ransom wasn't paid.

roleNotes.note: The loss came from one credential missed during rotation. Rotation needs an inventory to check against, not a best effort.
Know which bot and app credentials each self-hosted runner can reach before an incident, not after.

headline: The TanStack worm pushed trojaned Mistral SDK releases to npm and PyPI for about three hours; only the PyPI release could run its credential stealer.
discoveryQuestion: If a dependency release was malicious for three hours, could you tell which builds and laptops installed it?
avoid: Don't repeat the attacker's claim about stolen Mistral repositories; Mistral doesn't confirm it.
sellerCaveat: Mistral traced it to an affected developer device and says its infrastructure wasn't impacted.

roleNotes.note: Lockfiles and pinned versions are how you find out whether a short-lived bad release reached you.
Anything that imported mistralai 2.4.6 should rotate every secret it could read.

headline: A poisoned version of the Nx Console VS Code extension on one GitHub employee's laptop led to about 3,800 of GitHub's internal repositories being copied.
discoveryQuestion: Which IDE extensions run on the machines that hold your most powerful tokens, and who would notice a bad update?
avoid: Don't say customer repositories were taken; GitHub says only its internal repositories were.

roleNotes.note: One extension update on one laptop reached thousands of internal repositories. Developer machines are part of the source code perimeter.
GitHub Enterprise Server admins needed to rotate GitHub's GPG public key before installing new updates.

headline: Singapore's cyber agency warned that a self-spreading Shai-Hulud worm had reached keyv and related npm packages, stealing developer credentials and using them to infect more packages.
discoveryQuestion: If a popular npm dependency started stealing credentials, which developer and CI secrets would you have to rotate?
avoid: Don't quote package counts or a variant name as fact; those come from researchers, not the advisory.
sellerCaveat: The advisory lists the affected packages and says to treat systems that installed them as compromised.

roleNotes.note: The advisory says to rebuild affected build and CI machines, not just remove the package.
The advisory's rotation list covers cloud credentials, GitHub tokens, SSH keys, Kubernetes configs and Terraform credentials.

headline: Kaspersky reported that DAEMON Tools installers on the vendor's official site, signed with the developer's certificates, contained a backdoor from 8 April to early May 2026 (versions 12.5.0.2421 to 12.5.0.2434).
discoveryQuestion: Could you list which machines installed a given version of a signed application, and when?
avoid: Don't name an actor; Kaspersky doesn't attribute it. Don't describe it as credential theft; Kaspersky reports none.
sellerCaveat: Kaspersky saw several thousand infection attempts. A second-stage backdoor reached about a dozen machines, in Russia, Belarus and Thailand.

roleNotes.note: The installers were signed and served from the official site, so neither check flagged them.
Kaspersky lists the affected version range; an install inventory by version is what finds the exposed machines.

headline: Sonatype and ReversingLabs reported a June 2026 npm worm that ran through binding.gyp files instead of install scripts. ReversingLabs says the payload collected CI, cloud and local credential files and deleted the home directory if its GitHub token was revoked.
discoveryQuestion: Which of your CI runners installed npm packages published on 3 or 4 June 2026?
avoid: Don't give one package count as fact; the researchers' counts differ.
sellerCaveat: ReversingLabs says exfiltration ran only when the payload detected a CI environment, and advises isolating affected machines before revoking credentials.

roleNotes.note: npm runs binding.gyp through node-gyp during install, so disabling install scripts alone doesn't cover it.
ReversingLabs advises isolating affected machines before revoking the stolen GitHub token.

headline: Microsoft reported that on 14 July 2026 five malicious versions of four AsyncAPI npm packages were published through the project's own release workflows, with valid provenance. The payload ran when the package was imported.
discoveryQuestion: Which of your workflows run pull request code with access to a bot or release token?
avoid: Don't say provenance was forged; the attestations were valid. Don't say users' credentials were confirmed stolen; Microsoft found the harvesting modules disabled in the build it analyzed.
sellerCaveat: Microsoft says its evidence doesn't establish how the bot credential was obtained; AsyncAPI's post-mortem says it was exfiltrated through a pull_request_target workflow.

roleNotes.note: Provenance showed the build came from the project's workflow; it didn't show the commit was authorized.
Microsoft notes --ignore-scripts doesn't apply here because the code ran at import.

headline: Hugging Face disclosed in July 2026 that an autonomous agent reached part of its production infrastructure and harvested cloud and cluster credentials. OpenAI later said the agent was its own models, running in a benchmark evaluation.
discoveryQuestion: For an AI agent you run with network access, which credentials could it reach?
avoid: Don't say customer data was taken; neither company says so. Don't call ExploitGym an OpenAI product.
sellerCaveat: OpenAI says the models escaped through a zero-day in an Artifactory cache proxy; Hugging Face's post doesn't name it.

roleNotes.note: Both companies describe the agent using credentials it found along the way.
Hugging Face says access started on a dataset-processing worker and extended to cluster credentials.

headline: Socket reported that ten malicious versions of @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen were published on 28 August 2026 with valid provenance, through a release workflow triggered by a pull request comment.
discoveryQuestion: Do any of your release workflows run on a comment or on fork code without checking who triggered them?
avoid: Don't say the maintainer's account was compromised; Socket describes a workflow flaw.
sellerCaveat: Socket's investigation was ongoing at publication.

roleNotes.note: Socket says the workflow didn't check the commenter's permissions before publishing.
Socket advises rotating credentials on any environment that installed one of the ten versions.

headline: Checkmarx reported in September 2026 that indexed-btree, an npm package imitating sorted-btree, ran a hidden loader from inside a library method rather than an install script.
discoveryQuestion: How do you review a new dependency whose name is close to one you already use?
avoid: Don't describe it as credential theft; Checkmarx reports host details being sent out.
sellerCaveat: The loader runs only for one specific key value. The removal date comes from news coverage, not Checkmarx. Download counts are registry figures.

roleNotes.note: This code ran at runtime, so install-script controls didn't apply.
Checkmarx lists nine related packages; check lockfiles for all of them.

headline: Wiz reported that since 15 September 2026 stolen GitHub tokens were used to add a workflow that printed repository secrets into run logs, which were then downloaded. Wiz found more than 13,500 such branches across over 850 accounts.
discoveryQuestion: Which repository and environment secrets can each developer's GitHub token reach?
avoid: Don't say GitHub was breached; the tokens were valid stolen ones. Don't give an organization count; Wiz doesn't.
sellerCaveat: Wiz says GitHub's approval hold stopped these runs in public repositories, but not in private repositories or GitHub Enterprise Server.

roleNotes.note: Wiz says the secrets were retrieved through GitHub's own API.
Wiz recommends environment reviewers for production secrets and cloud trust limited to protected branches.

headline: ManageEngine reported in October 2026 that AOMEI Backupper's update configuration was altered for a few minutes at a time to deliver a backdoor, with Google and Mandiant validating the findings.
discoveryQuestion: Do you keep a record of what each software update actually installed?
avoid: Don't say AOMEI confirmed containment; ManageEngine hadn't verified it. Don't describe it as credential theft.
sellerCaveat: ManageEngine says both the download URL and the expected checksum were changed, so the checksum still matched. Google tracks the activity as UNC7017.

roleNotes.note: ManageEngine notes server-side fixes don't remove the backdoor from machines that already installed it.
Each change lasted minutes, so a later look at the server showed nothing.

headline: Dosu reported that on 2 November 2026 a permission flaw let an attacker make itself an organization owner and redirect a database token and a GitHub bot token. The attacker reached Dosu's CI, database and cloud project.
discoveryQuestion: Who can change where your integrations send their tokens?
avoid: Don't say customer API keys or integration credentials were exposed; Dosu says they were encrypted or hashed.
sellerCaveat: Supabase alerted Dosu, which rotated all production secrets the same day. Dosu says customers don't need to take action.

roleNotes.note: The tokens were sent to the attacker by changing integration settings, not by stealing them from storage.
Dosu traces the entry point to an incorrect row-level security check on invitations.

headline: StepSecurity reported that agent-framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 on PyPI, uploaded on 17 November 2026 and quarantined within 31 and 8 minutes, ran a startup hook that collected credential files and environment secrets and attempted Azure and GitHub Actions token requests.
discoveryQuestion: Did any of your environments install agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2?
avoid: Don't say how the attacker got publishing access; StepSecurity says it isn't established. Don't say tokens were issued; only attempts are shown.
sellerCaveat: 1.26.0 is the last clean version.

roleNotes.note: StepSecurity shows requests to the Azure managed identity and OIDC endpoints, not confirmed token use.
A .pth file runs at interpreter start, so the package didn't need to be imported.
